predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2 (text preceding Definition 2.3): "This condition forces L to be a univalent function."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The hypotheses are: S is a nowhere-vanishing exact holomorphic 1-form and L(x)=∫_o^x S has x=o as its only zero. These give that L is locally injective (L'=S≠0) with a single zero, which does NOT imply global injectivity. Counterexample: on S=𝔻 take L(z)=((1-z)^{-3}-1)/3, so L'=(1-z)^{-4} never vanishes, the only zero of L in 𝔻 is z=0 (the other cube roots give |1-ω|=√3>1), yet L is not injective on 𝔻 (ζ=1/(1-z) covers Re ζ>1/2, and ζ↦ζ³ is not injective there). Univalence of L is used later (simple connectivity of D^S(r), C^S(r) a simple closed curve), so this is a genuine gap, not a typo.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, after Definition 2.4: "Since L is univalent, then D^S(r) is simply connected for all r>0" (and the subsequent claim that C^S(r) is a simple closed curve)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Even if L were univalent, D^S(r)≅L(S)∩{|w|<r} need not be connected or simply connected: e.g. if L(S)={|w|<3}∖{|w−2|≤1/2}, then L(S)∩{|w|<3} is not simply connected. No argument is supplied, yet these topological facts underlie the identification of C^S(r) as a single simple closed curve on which the harmonic measure is computed.

For u(x)=|x̂| one has |∇u|_h = ‖S‖_h (exactly the computation of Lemma 2.12), so the correct identity is ∫_{D^S(r)} k dV = ∫_0^r dt ∫_{C^S(t)} k ‖S‖_h^{-1} dσ_t. Consequently the inequality d/dr(rA_k') ≥ (2πr/‖S‖_{r,sup})E_k(r) should read with ‖S‖²_{r,sup}, and Lemma 3.6 should carry ‖S‖²_{r,sup}. predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof uses ∫_{C^S(r)} k dσ_r ≥ (2πr/‖S‖_{r,sup}) E_k(r), which follows from dπ_o^r=‖S‖_h dσ_r/(2πr) only when k ≥ 0; for sign-changing k the inequality is false. (i) The step replaces N_f(r,ζ) by T+O(1) inside an integral against K'ω with an inequality, but the First Main Theorem gives N ≤ T+O(1); this only yields the displayed '≥' if K' ≤ 0 everywhere, which is not assumed (ω is an arbitrary positive (1,1)-form, and for g=0, K'>0). predicted_errors.error_location: Lemma 2.12 and the formula dπ_o^r(x) = −½ ∂g_r(o,x)/∂n dσ_r(x) (Section 2, 'Harmonic measures on S-circles')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The normal is twice declared to be the inward normal, but (a) Green's identity gives dπ = −½ ∂g/∂ν dσ with ν the OUTWARD normal (with the inward normal the sign would make the harmonic measure negative), and (b) the vector exhibited in the proof, ∇|L|/|∇|L||, points in the direction of increasing |L|, i.e. outward. The two sign errors cancel, but the statement as written is incorrect. In addition, setting 'h|_{x_0}=1' and concluding |φ(x_0)|=‖S_{x_0}‖_h is inconsistent with the convention dV=√−1 h dz∧dz̄ (which corresponds to ds²=2h|dz|²), introducing a spurious √2.

"Let {r_n} be a sequence of positive integers r_n with r_1<r_2<… and r_n → R^S": a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers cannot converge to a finite R^S (and the whole point of the hyperbolic case is R^S<∞). The hypothesis must be a sequence of positive real numbers.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 3.4 (and Theorem 3.7 / item 13) versus Theorem I, Corollaries I–II and the proof
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem I is announced as being Theorem 3.4 and has the truncated counting functions ∑ \overline{N}_f^S(r,a_j) on the right-hand side, as does the proof (which passes from ∑N_f − N(r,D_ram) to ∑\overline{N}_f). But Theorem 3.4 and Theorem 3.7 are stated with the untruncated ∑N_f^S(r,a_j). This is a substantive discrepancy: the defect relation of Corollary 3.8/Theorem III is formulated with the simple defect \overline{δ}_f (defined via \overline{N}) and does not follow from the version of Theorem 3.7 as stated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1, after (3): "If f is nonconstant, then we can check T_{f,ω}^S(r) ≥ O(log r). By using the First Main Theorem … 0 ≤ \overline{δ}_f(a) ≤ 1."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The bound 'T ≥ O(log r)' is both formally meaningless (O(·) on the smaller side of an inequality) and useless in the hyperbolic case R^S<∞, where log r stays bounded. To guarantee 0 ≤ \overline{δ}_f(a) ≤ 1 one needs T_{f,ω}^S(r) → ∞ as r→R^S, which is false for e.g. a nonconstant bounded holomorphic function on the dz-exhausted disc 𝔻 (T stays bounded, and then the O(1) in N ≤ T+O(1) is not negligible). Hence the asserted range of the defect, and with it the defect relations of Theorem III/Corollary 3.8, are not established in the hyperbolic case.

predicted_errors.error_location: Hypothesis on γ in Theorem I, Theorem II, Theorem 3.4, Lemma 3.5, Lemma 3.6, Theorem 4.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: "Let γ be an integrable function on (0,R^S) with ∫_0^{R^S} γ(r) dr = ∞" is self-contradictory as written (an integrable function has finite integral). The intended hypothesis is that γ is positive and locally integrable with divergent total integral; as stated the hypotheses of all the main theorems are vacuous.

predicted_errors.error_location: Title vs. body of the paper
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper is titled 'Nevanlinna Theory on Geodesic Balls of Complete Kähler Manifolds', but the article header and all of the content concern 'Nevanlinna theory via holomorphic forms' on S-exhausted Riemann surfaces; geodesic balls of Kähler manifolds appear only in the Motivation as prior work [4] (which the paper explicitly moves away from, since here the exhaustion is by S-discs, not geodesic balls).

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, sentence introducing Proposition 2.1: "Gunning proved that: Proposition 2.1 (Gunning and Narasimhan [6])"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The cited existence theorem for a nowhere-vanishing exact holomorphic 1-form on an open Riemann surface is the joint result of Gunning and Narasimhan (Immersion of open Riemann surfaces, Math. Ann. 1967); attributing it to Gunning alone in the text contradicts the citation given in the very next line.

predicted_errors.error_location: Paragraph preceding the lower bound for T^S(r,ℛ): "By uniformization theorem, for each nonnegative constant C, there exists a metric h such that the Gauss curvature K satisfies −C ≤ K ≤ 0."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The uniformization theorem produces complete metrics of constant curvature 0, 1 or −1 on the universal cover; it does not yield, for every nonnegative C (in particular C=0, which forces K≡0), a metric with −C ≤ K ≤ 0 on an arbitrary open Riemann surface. (A flat metric does exist here, but because of the nowhere-vanishing form S, not because of uniformization.) The justification given is therefore invalid.
